rv.q: This play is both a Hallelujah and an A-men.
The play provides audiences with the blessed release of almost continual laughter, which is something we probably all need.

In the comic scenes, when the sisters are eyeing each other’s outfits or Logan is bobbling his Bible, the play stands on solid ground, but in the long-seeming resolution scenes, as the drama comes to rely on plot developments, the journey toward uplift turns convenient and then mechanical.
Whether it succeeds for you will depend largely on your taste for Broadway comedies of a type that otherwise went out of style a few decades ago.
The enthusiasm to bring Chicken & Biscuits to Broadway is understandable, but audiences paying these prices have the right to expect something less undercooked.
If all that happened, we'd have an entertaining show aimed at a popular audience.
Unfortunately, while Chicken and Biscuits promises romp and chaos, the play’s formulaic script feels like a drawn-out sitcom, having a more soporific effect.
If theater lovers are smart, they’ll heed the call and go straight to Chicken & Biscuits church.
Refreshingly, in this laughter-rich script, and under Zhailon Levington's sparkling direction, the experience eschews the pitfalls of typical media portrayals of Black tragedy in favor of Black joy.
Still, with the cast having this much fun onstage, it’s hard not to feel like part of the family, and Chicken & Biscuits is comfort food worth reheating.

But it’s also full of laughs, performed by a great, eight-member cast that includes popular Broadway pros Norm Lewis and Michael Urie, as well as five performers making their Broadway debuts, including Ebony Marshall
But unfortunately, it is cliched and tedious, with numerous scenes that drag on endlessly.
Death is easy, comedy is hard, and milking laughs at a funeral is nearly impossible.
Like grandpa’s biscuits, stale is the word that comes to mind.
How much you enjoy the evening will depend on your tolerance for stereotypical characterizations and situations more redolent of a sitcom than theater.
Under the direction of debuting director Zhailon Levingston, the fine cast makes the play seem better than it is and offers many new faces to the Broadway stage.
Chicken and Biscuits fulfills its promise. It is two hours of soulful, side-splitting fun.
The play is, above all, meant to be comfort food for the soul, and audiences who come prepared to eat it all up are sure to leave satisfied.
There seems to be an equal balance of both.
We are pummeled into laughing submission, unable to question in real time what we are laughing at, and more importantly whom.
You can mash, fry, boil, and bake Chicken and Biscuits but it still doesn’t make a very good play.
Chicken and Biscuits suffers from a tedious, drawn-out structure
